title: Monte Carlo reconstruction of symmetry-twisted partition function ratios: the critical 3D Ising
abstract: We introduce a Monte Carlo strategy for directly estimating partition function ratios between distinct global sectors of a lattice theory. It enlarges the configuration space to sample an interpolating family whose endpoints are the desired sectors, and uses flat histogram methods to reconstruct the corresponding free energy difference. Although the construction is more general, we focus here on the three-dimensional Ising model on the slab $\mathbb{R}^{2}\times S^{1}_{L_{z}}$ at the bulk critical point, comparing the untwisted periodic sector with the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-twisted antiperiodic sector. A large-volume and aspect ratio extrapolation gives the symmetry-twisted thermodynamic Casimir difference $Δ_{\mathbb{Z}_{2}}=0.327(2)$ directly, without lattice derivatives or bulk subtractions. This provides an independent twisted sector probe of tensions observed in periodic sector thermodynamic Casimir observables. More generally, the method gives direct but selective numerical access to CFT compactification data, including estimates of the effective thermal screening scale and the $\mathbb{Z}_{2}$-odd sector energy gap on $T^{2}$.
summary: This paper introduces a powerful Monte Carlo technique to calculate free energy differences between distinct global sectors in lattice field theories. Applied to the 3D Ising model, it yields an independent measurement of the symmetry-twisted Casimir difference ($\Delta Z_2$). This method provides a robust tool for probing universal CFT data by analyzing finite-size effects across different geometric limits.
main_problem: The primary goal is to estimate partition function ratios between distinct global sectors of a lattice theory, specifically focusing on symmetry-twisted observables.
main_result: The authors directly calculate the symmetry-twisted thermodynamic Casimir difference ($\Delta Z_2 = 0.327(2)$) for the critical 3D Ising model without needing lattice derivatives or bulk subtractions.
method: A Monte Carlo strategy is employed by enlarging the configuration space to sample an interpolating family between the desired sectors, using flat histogram methods to reconstruct the free energy difference.
model_or_system: The study focuses on the three-dimensional Ising model simulated on a slab geometry ($R^2 	imes S^1_{L_z}$) at its bulk critical point. The comparison is made between the standard periodic sector and the $\mathbb{Z}_2$-twisted antiperiodic sector.
key_observables: Symmetry-twisted thermodynamic Casimir difference ($\Delta Z_2$), sector free energy difference ($\Delta F_{Z_2}$), and finite-size gap parameters ($\kappa_\sigma$).
important_parameters: The aspect ratio $q = L/L_z$, the lattice size ($L, L_z$), and the coupling variable $J$ used for interpolation.
main_assumptions: The analysis relies on large-volume and aspect ratio extrapolations to extract universal continuum limits. The method assumes that sector differences allow access to CFT compactification data.
figures_summary: Figures illustrate benchmarks (e.g., 2D case approaching $\pi/4$) and the convergence of observables ($\Delta Z_2$ and gap parameters) as system sizes are taken to their thermodynamic limits via various extrapolation ansätze.
paper_structure: The paper develops a general Monte Carlo method for sector ratio estimation, applies it specifically to the 3D Ising model on a slab geometry, analyzes the large-$q$ limit to find $\Delta Z_2$, and then examines the small-$q$ channel to determine spectral gaps ($\kappa_\sigma$).
why_interesting: While focused on classical statistical mechanics, the use of advanced Monte Carlo techniques (flat histograms) and connections to CFT/spectral analysis are highly relevant for understanding quantum many-body systems where finite-size effects and boundary conditions dictate low-energy physics.

figures.caption: Figure 1. Two-dimensional benchmark of the flat histogram estimator. The dimensionless differ- ence Lz∆fZ2(L, Lz) is plotted against q = L/Lz for several transverse sizes L. The dashed line is the conformal result Lz∆fZ2 →π/4 at q, Lz →∞. The black dotted curve is the exact Ising torus result from the Jacobi-theta representation of the Virasoro characters [23]. Dashed curves are cubic interpolations in q at fixed L. The gray band marks the large-q window used below, to study finite-L effects. The deviations at small Lz/large-q are the lattice and finite-volume corrections discussed in the text.

Figure 2. Finite-q corrections in the two-dimensional benchmark. The plot shows Lz∆fZ2(L, Lz)− π/4 versus q = L/Lz. The dashed curves are the leading large-q and small-q exponential approxi- mations. The exponential regime is visible only after the small-Lz lattice corrections are controlled.

Figure 3. Large-q extrapolation at fixed Lz. For each q ∈[16, 100], the interpolation is evaluated and plotted versus Lz, as a single data set. This range makes exponential finite-q corrections negligible, as indicated by fig. 2. Raw data at aspect ratios with at least four values of Lz are also shown. The convergence from q = 4 to q = 8 and the stability at q ≳16 indicate that the interpolation is in the asymptotic regime.

Figure 4. Raw finite-volume data for the three-dimensional slab at β = βc = 0.221654626(5). The plot shows Y (L, Lz) = L2 z∆fZ2(L, Lz) versus q = L/Lz for several transverse sizes L. Dashed curves are cubic interpolations in q at fixed L. The dashed black line is the infinite volume extrapolation. The gray band marks the large-q window used for the fixed-Lz diagnostic in fig. 5. Unlike the two dimensional case, there is no clear plateau.

Figure 5. Large-q evaluation of the three-dimensional slab data at fixed Lz. For each Lz, the interpolation is evaluated at q = L/Lz ∈[8, 16], where finite-q corrections are not visible within the statistical precision. The values are plotted versus Lz and show the finite-Lz approach to the slab Casimir amplitude. Raw data at fixed aspect ratios with several Lz values are also shown. A free power-law fit gives an effective exponent near 2.5; the second fit includes terms proportional to L−(∆T ′−3) z , L−(∆ϵ′−3) z , and L−2 z .
